title: Rav Zutra bar Tuviah
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: He was Rav’s student, as we find “Rav Zutra bar Tuviah said that Rav said” in Berakhot 7a and 43b, Shabbat 75a, Pesachim 87a, Yoma 39b, Taanit 16b, Chagigah 12a and 13b, Nedarim 41b, Bava Metzia 59a, Bava Batra 97a, Sanhedrin 106a, Avodah Zarah 24b, Makkot 6b and 12a, Zevachim 64b and Menachot 11a. Afterward he sat before Rav Yehudah, as in Moed Katan 16b, where he was reciting the Scripture lesson before Rav Yehudah; Zutra asked Rav Yehudah, who did not answer; Zutra asked a second time. Rav Yehudah said: “Because he does not know the explanation of this verse, is he not a great man?” He realized that he had taken the matter to heart (that Rav Yehudah was angry with him), and Rav Zutra bar Tuviah observed a period of admonition for himself for one day. We likewise find “Rav Zutra bar Tuviah said that Rav Nachman said,” as in Yoma 86b.

His halakhot we find in Yevamot 44a, where he said that he does not perform chalitzah for both, for the verse says “the house of the one whose shoe was removed”; in Gittin 86b he raises an objection to Rav’s words; and in Menachot 11a he challenges Rabbi Elazar’s words. Hyman notes that for the most part it is written “Rav Zutra bar Tuviah” with a heh, which Hyman takes to distinguish him from the later Rav Zutra bar Tuvia, which is with an aleph.

notes.text: פסק סידרא means reciting a Scripture lesson, not dividing verses. Saved Davidson Moed Katan16b shows Zutra asking and Yehudah declining to answer, then Zutra observing a one-day nezifah, an admonition rather than formal excommunication. Hyman’s heh/aleph spelling distinction remains his claim, without global identity binding.

Moed Katan 16b directly has Zutra reciting Scripture, asking Yehudah twice and observing a one-day nezifah after the rebuke. This is an admonition rather than formal excommunication. Hyman’s heh-versus-aleph name-spelling distinction remains his argument, not a global identity rule.
